## Overview

Build a k-NN classifier using tidymodels on the penguins dataset. Use cross-validation to tune k.

## Task 1: Build and Tune k-NN

```{r}
library(tidymodels)
library(palmerpenguins)

penguins_clean <- penguins |> drop_na()
split <- initial_split(penguins_clean, prop = 0.8, strata = species)
train <- training(split); test <- testing(split)

knn_spec <- nearest_neighbor(neighbors = tune()) |>
  set_engine("kknn") |> set_mode("classification")

rec <- recipe(species ~ bill_length_mm + bill_depth_mm + flipper_length_mm + body_mass_g,
              data = train) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

wf <- workflow() |> add_model(knn_spec) |> add_recipe(rec)

# Tune k with 5-fold CV
tune_results <- tune_grid(
  wf, resamples = vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = species),
  grid = tibble(neighbors = c(1, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 15, 21))
)

autoplot(tune_results)
show_best(tune_results, metric = "accuracy")
```

**Your turn:** Which k gave the best CV accuracy? Why might k=1 be a bad choice even if its training accuracy is high?

> *The best k is k = 5, with a mean CV accuracy of about 0.989 (and a standard error of about 0.0076). Accuracy falls off for larger k (0.985 at k=7, 0.977 at k=21). The Brier score is also lowest around k=5–7, and ROC AUC is essentially perfect from k=5 on. k=1 is a bad choice even with higher accuracy, as with k=1, each prediction copies the single nearest neighbor, so the model memorizes the training data.*

## Task 2: Final Model on Test Set

```{r}
best_k <- select_best(tune_results, metric = "accuracy")
final_wf <- finalize_workflow(wf, best_k)
final_fit <- final_wf |> fit(data = train)

test_preds <- predict(final_fit, test) |> bind_cols(test)
accuracy(test_preds, truth = species, estimate = .pred_class)
```

## Task 3: Compare to Logistic Regression

Fit a multinomial logistic regression on the same data. Which performs better?

```{r}
# Your comparison code here
log_spec <- multinom_reg() |>
  set_engine("nnet") |> set_mode("classification")

log_wf <- workflow() |> add_model(log_spec) |> add_recipe(rec)

log_cv <- fit_resamples(
  log_wf, resamples = vfold_cv(train, v = 5, strata = species),
  metrics = metric_set(accuracy)
)
collect_metrics(log_cv)

# Test-set accuracy
log_fit <- fit(log_wf, data = train)
log_preds <- predict(log_fit, test) |> bind_cols(test)
accuracy(log_preds, truth = species, estimate = .pred_class)
```

**Your turn:** Which model had higher test accuracy? Which would you choose if interpretability matters?

> *Both models reached 100% test accuracy, so they tied. In CV, KNN (k=5) scored 0.989 vs. 0.977 for logistic regression, a gap of roughly 1.5 standard errors, so the difference is weak and the small test set can’t separate them. If interpretability matters, I’d choose logistic regression: its coefficients show how each measurement shifts the odds of each species, whereas KNN has no parameters to inspect. With comparable performance, the simpler, more interpretable model is the better trade-off.*
